_description: Supporting evidence from bike-share systems in other cities. New York City (Citi Bike) is excluded because it is the target market, not a case study. Financial results marked null are not publicly available — display as 'Not publicly available'. Do not invent missing metrics.

case_studies.government_involvement: SFMTA treats Bay Wheels as public transit infrastructure — integrated into route planning, subsidized station buildouts, protected bike lanes, and joint fare programs.
case_studies.investment_action: SFMTA funded station expansion in underserved neighborhoods and built protected cycling infrastructure connecting Bay Wheels stations to transit hubs.
case_studies.ridership_result: Strong per-station utilization comparable to much larger systems, driven by transit integration and government support.
case_studies.fleet_growth: Expanded from ~300 stations in 2019 to ~800 stations by 2026, including significant e-bike fleet growth.
case_studies.station_growth: Station count grew approximately 2.7x over 7 years with government co-funding.
case_studies.major_milestone: Full integration with SFMTA transit planning — Bay Wheels appears on official transit maps alongside Muni and BART.
case_studies.main_lesson: Government partnership transforms bike-share from a private amenity into public transit infrastructure, unlocking ridership and station growth that private investment alone cannot achieve.

case_studies.government_involvement: Ile-de-France Mobilites (regional transit authority) fully funds and governs the system. The city owns all stations and infrastructure.
case_studies.investment_action: Complete system overhaul in 2018 — replaced operator, expanded to 1,400+ stations across the greater Paris metropolitan area, added 40% e-bikes.
case_studies.ridership_result: Over 400,000 trips per day at peak, making it one of the world's largest and most-used bike-share systems.
case_studies.fleet_growth: 20,000+ bikes including approximately 8,000 e-bikes across the system.
case_studies.station_growth: Expanded from ~1,200 stations under the original Velib to over 1,400 stations under the new contract, extending beyond Paris city limits.
case_studies.major_milestone: Survived a difficult operator transition in 2018 and rebounded to higher ridership than the original system, proving resilience of government-owned infrastructure.
case_studies.main_lesson: Government ownership of infrastructure ensures system continuity even when operators change. E-bike integration dramatically increased ridership and willingness to cycle longer distances.

case_studies.government_involvement: Transport for London (TfL) owns and governs the entire system. Santander provides title sponsorship. TfL sets pricing, expansion plans, and integrates the system with Oyster/contactless fare payment.
case_studies.investment_action: TfL expanded from 6,000 bikes and 400 docking stations at launch (2010) to over 12,000 bikes and 800 stations, with eastward expansion into underserved boroughs.
case_studies.ridership_result: Over 10 million rides per year consistently. Record ridership months during transit strikes and good weather periods.
case_studies.fleet_growth: Doubled fleet size from 6,000 to 12,000+ bikes over the system's lifetime.
case_studies.station_growth: Grew from 400 to 800+ docking stations with ongoing eastward expansion.
case_studies.major_milestone: Integrated with Oyster and contactless payment, making it seamless to use alongside Tube, buses, and rail — a model for true multimodal integration.
case_studies.main_lesson: Full integration with the city's transit payment system removes friction and drives adoption. Government ownership allows long-term planning and expansion into areas a purely commercial operator might avoid.

case_studies.government_involvement: BIXI is operated by a publicly owned non-profit corporation created by the City of Montreal. The city provides infrastructure support, road access, and integration with public transit planning.
case_studies.investment_action: After near-bankruptcy in 2014, the city restructured BIXI as a public corporation with new governance. Since then, the system has expanded aggressively with e-bikes and new stations.
case_studies.ridership_result: Record-breaking ridership year after year — over 8 million trips in 2023, up from approximately 4 million in 2017.
case_studies.fleet_growth: Grew from approximately 5,000 bikes to over 10,000 including 2,600+ e-bikes.
case_studies.station_growth: Expanded from approximately 460 stations to over 800 stations across Montreal and surrounding municipalities.
case_studies.financial_result: BIXI reported its first operating surplus in 2022 after years of government-backed restructuring, demonstrating that public bike-share can become self-sustaining.
case_studies.major_milestone: BIXI's turnaround from near-bankruptcy to operating surplus is the strongest public evidence that government intervention can save and grow a bike-share system.
case_studies.main_lesson: Government intervention during financial distress can save a bike-share system and set it on a path to self-sustainability. Public ownership aligns incentives with ridership growth rather than short-term profit.

case_studies.government_involvement: Jointly funded by Washington D.C., Arlington County, Alexandria, and Montgomery County. The District Department of Transportation (DDOT) oversees planning and expansion. Stations are placed on public land by government decision.
case_studies.investment_action: Multi-jurisdictional government partnership funded station expansion across the D.C. metro area, with dedicated funding for equity programs in underserved neighborhoods.
case_studies.ridership_result: Over 4 million trips per year, making it one of the top five bike-share systems in North America.
case_studies.fleet_growth: Grew from approximately 1,100 bikes at launch (2010) to over 5,000 bikes including e-bikes.
case_studies.station_growth: Expanded from approximately 110 stations to over 700 stations spanning four jurisdictions.
case_studies.major_milestone: Successfully operates across four separate government jurisdictions with a unified system — a model for regional bike-share coordination.
case_studies.main_lesson: Cross-jurisdictional government cooperation enables seamless bike-share across metro areas. Equity-focused expansion funded by government ensures bike-share serves all communities, not just affluent urban cores.
